低音哨笛以哨笛原理發聲，屬端吹哨口笛；最低音通常為中央C上方的G或更低，常見型比: The low whistle sounds on the whistle principle, as an end-blown duct flute; its lowest note is usually G above middle C or lower, and the common type sounds an octave below the traditional D whistle. It has appeared with Tommy Makem, Finbar Furey, Michael McGoldrick, Davy Spillane, Riverdance and Lunasa. The Riverdance tours of the 1990s took it beyond traditional music; Spillane has blended it with modern jazz and rhythm and blues; in rock, Troy Donockley plays it occasionally with the symphonic metal band Nightwish, and Jeroen Goossens has used it in Arjen Lucassen's Ayreon project.

In late 1971 the English flute maker Bernard Overton, working with Finbar Furey, made the first modern low whistle, copying in metal a bamboo flute of Furey's that had been damaged, then changing to all aluminium, and producing instruments in A, G and low D. The name 'Irish low whistle' does not describe its origin but its heavy use in Ireland and the British Isles; the Riverdance tours of the 1990s gave it commercial exposure.

The low whistle is a variant of the traditional tin whistle or penny whistle, with a lower range and a larger body, in the end-blown duct flute family, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.221.1. Its lowest note is usually G above middle C or lower, commonly low D, an octave below the traditional D whistle. The principle and the fingering are much the same as the traditional whistle's, but because the holes are further apart players often need the piper's grip to cover the holes. It is common on slow airs in Celtic music, and also in jigs, reels and hornpipes in Ireland, Scotland, the Isle of Man, Wales and England, played by Tommy Makem, Finbar Furey, Michael McGoldrick, Riverdance, Lunasa, Donie Keyes, Chris Conway, Davy Spillane and others.
